relationship_to_restored_text: Interpretive contemplative layer aligned by verse. This does not replace the source-audited restored translation.

verses.mystical_translation: Azariah's long reign begins while another king's calendar is counted.
A sixteen-year-old enters fifty-two years of rule, with his mother named beside him.
The narrator remembers a largely faithful path.
Local worship remains beyond the king's reform.
Chronic skin disease changes the king's residence, and governance is shared with his son.
The royal archive holds the rest of his life beyond illness.
He is buried among his ancestors, and Jotham succeeds.
Zechariah receives only six months on the northern throne.
The inherited political-religious pattern persists.
Shallum kills him publicly and takes the throne.
The record keeps what the short reign barely had time to become.
Four generations complete Jehu's dynastic promise.
Shallum's reign lasts one month.
Menahem answers one coup with another killing.
Conspiracy becomes the main achievement preserved for Shallum.
A city that will not open is subjected to massacre and violence against pregnant bodies.
Menahem's ten-year reign rises from that terror.
No length of rule transforms the system he continues.
Assyrian power arrives, and silver purchases support for the throne.
Wealth is extracted from subjects to stabilize one ruler's position.
The official archive records Menahem's remaining acts.
His son inherits the kingdom.
Pekahiah receives two years in Samaria.
The old pattern again survives the new name.
A palace officer and fifty armed men kill the king inside his citadel.
The royal record closes another shortened life.
Pekah begins twenty years of rule.
The inherited evaluation remains unchanged.
Assyria takes cities and carries whole communities away from home.
Hoshea's conspiracy kills Pekah and repeats the cycle.
The record absorbs another coup into chronology.
Jotham's southern reign begins amid northern instability.
His age, years, and mother anchor the king in ordinary human time.
He follows the better parts of his father's way.
High places continue while he builds a temple gate.
The archive holds the rest of his work.
Aram and Israel begin pressing Judah.
Jotham dies, is buried, and Ahaz inherits the gathering crisis.

contemplative_note: The chapter races through kings because violence has made the throne unstable. Against that blur, certain bodies must not disappear: a chronically ill king, pregnant people attacked in Tiphsah, wealthy subjects taxed for regime protection, and communities deported by Assyria. Political chronology is never more important than the human lives it compresses.
